mainTopic: How רבי could plant on פורים (which day, and whether work is forbidden at all), and the doubtful walled status of טבריה and הוצל
overview: This amud finishes רבי אלעזר's report that רבי planted on פורים, bathed in public on שבעה עשר בתמוז, and tried to abolish תשעה באב. רבי אבא בר זבדא corrects him: רבי only wanted to drop תשעה באב in a year when it fell on שבת and had already been postponed. The גמרא then asks how רבי could plant on פורים, since רב יוסף taught that work is forbidden. After some back-and-forth, it answers that רבי lived in walled טבריה, kept the 15th, and planted on the 14th. Eulogies and fasting are forbidden on both days, but work is forbidden only on one's own day. רבה בריה דרבא gives a bolder answer: the people never accepted a ban on work on פורים at all, because 'יום טוב' is missing from the final פסוק. רב's curse on a man who planted flax is explained as a local custom not to work, or else רבי's planting was a joyful 'planting of joy.' The גמרא then asks why חזקיה was unsure about טבריה. The sea formed one of its walls, and it is unclear whether a walled city for the מגילה is defined by being protected or by not being exposed. The amud ends with רב אסי's doubt about הוצל and the opening of a childhood story told by רבי יוחנן, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי bathed on שבעה עשר בתמוז and sought to uproot תשעה באב
steps.stepSummary: This finishes רבי אלעזר's report. רבי bathed publicly on שבעה עשר בתמוז and tried to abolish תשעה באב, but the חכמים did not agree.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he bathed at the busy wagon-market of צפורי on שבעה עשר בתמוז. He also tried to uproot the fast of תשעה באב, but they did not agree with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a report, begun on the previous amud, about unusual things רבי did on special days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי bathed in a very public place on שבעה עשר בתמוז, so people would see that bathing is allowed on that fast. He also wanted to abolish תשעה באב, and on that point the חכמים refused to go along. The planting on פורים, mentioned earlier in this report, is taken up starting in Step 4.

keyTerms.meaning: The wagon-market of צפורי, a busy and public place
The fast of the 17th of תמוז
They did not agree with him

steps.confusionAlert: This line starts in the middle of a sentence. The speaker is רבי אלעזר, and the subject 'he' is רבי (רבי יהודה הנשיא). The first part of the report, that he planted on פורים, came on the previous amud.

phrases.english: And he bathed at the wagon-market of Tzippori
on the seventeenth of Tammuz,
and he sought to uproot the Ninth of Av —
and they did not agree with him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the report of רבי אלעזר that began on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי showed that bathing is allowed on שבעה עשר בתמוז, and he tried to abolish תשעה באב, but the חכמים rejected that.

steps.title: רבי אבא בר זבדא corrects the story
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא בר זבדא says the story did not happen that way. רבי only wanted to cancel תשעה באב in one year, when it fell on שבת and was postponed. Even then, the חכמים did not agree.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא בר זבדא said before him: 'My teacher, that is not how it happened. It was a year when תשעה באב fell on שבת, and we postponed it to after שבת. רבי said: since it was already pushed off, let it be pushed off completely. And the חכמים did not agree.'
steps.whatsHappening: Someone who knew the real story steps in. He corrects the report about תשעה באב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The correction makes רבי's view much smaller. He never wanted to abolish תשעה באב forever. He only reasoned that in a year when the fast was already moved off its date because of שבת, it could be dropped for that year. The חכמים still disagreed, but the claim is now limited to that one unusual case.

keyTerms.meaning: That is not how the event happened
That happened to fall on שבת
Since it was pushed off, let it be pushed off entirely

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רבי never meant to cancel the fast of תשעה באב in general. He only suggested dropping it in a year when it had already been postponed.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לְפָנָיו רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר זַבְדָּא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda said before him:
phrases.notes: Before רבי אלעזר, who told the story.

phrases.english: My teacher, the event was not like this.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא תִּשְׁעָה בְּאָב שֶׁחָל לִהְיוֹת בְּשַׁבָּת הֲוָה,
phrases.english: Rather, it was a Ninth of Av that fell on Shabbat,
and we postponed it to after Shabbat.
And Rebbi said: since it was pushed off, let it be pushed off (entirely),
and the Sages did not agree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects and narrows the תשעה באב part of the report in step 1.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the claim that רבי tried to abolish תשעה באב altogether.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The report left out the key detail that the fast fell on שבת that year and had already been postponed.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר accepts the correction
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר praises the correction with the פסוק 'Two are better than one.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He applied to him the verse: 'Two are better than one.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר accepts the corrected version of the story. He says it is good that a second person was there to get the details right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Quoting the פסוק from קהלת shows that רבי אלעזר is happy to be corrected. The corrected version now stands: רבי's idea applied only to a postponed תשעה באב.

keyTerms.meaning: He applied a verse to him
Two are better than one (קהלת ד:ט)

phrases.english: He read about him:
"Two are better than one."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the correction made in step 2.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The corrected story stands: רבי only wanted to cancel a תשעה באב that had already been pushed off because of שבת.

steps.title: How could רבי plant on פורים if work is forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the planting. רב יוסף taught that the word 'יום טוב' in the מגילה forbids work on פורים, so how could רבי plant on that day?
steps.simpleTranslation: How could רבי plant a sapling on פורים? Didn't רב יוסף teach: 'gladness and feasting and a good day.' 'Gladness' teaches that eulogies are forbidden. 'Feasting' teaches that fasting is forbidden. 'A good day' teaches that doing work is forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now goes back to the first part of the story, the planting on פורים. It challenges that part using a teaching of רב יוסף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף reads three words in the פסוק in מגילת אסתר (ט:יט) as three separate rules. 'שמחה' rules out eulogies (הספד). 'משתה' rules out fasting (תענית). 'יום טוב' rules out work (מלאכה), just as on a festival. Planting counts as מלאכה, so רבי's act looks forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: A sapling, or the act of planting
But didn't he teach? (introduces a challenge from a teaching)

phrases.english: And how could Rebbi plant a sapling on Purim?
But didn't Rav Yosef teach:
"Gladness and feasting and a good day,"
"gladness" teaches that eulogies are forbidden,
"feasting" teaches that fasting is forbidden,
"and a good day" teaches that doing work is forbidden!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the תשעה באב discussion and returns to the planting part of the original report.
steps.kashyaTarget: The report that רבי planted a sapling on פורים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Planting is מלאכה, and רב יוסף derives from 'יום טוב' that מלאכה is forbidden on פורים.

steps.title: רבי kept the 14th and planted on the 15th
steps.stepSummary: First answer: רבי lived in a place that keeps פורים on the 14th, and he planted on the 15th, which was not his פורים day.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: רבי was a 'fourteenth' person, and when he planted, he planted on the fifteenth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי planted on the date that was not פורים for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unwalled towns keep פורים on the 14th of Adar, and walled cities keep it on the 15th. If רבי kept the 14th, then the 15th was an ordinary workday for him, so planting was allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who keeps פורים on the 14th

phrases.english: Rather: Rebbi was a "fourteenth" person,
and when he planted — he planted on the fifteenth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the planting was not on רבי's own פורים day.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We assumed רבי planted on the very day he kept as פורים.
steps.terutzMaskana: He kept the 14th and planted on the 15th, an ordinary day for him.

steps.title: But רבי lived in walled טבריה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects that answer. רבי lived in טבריה, which has been walled since the days of יהושע בן נון, so he must have kept the 15th.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רבי was in טבריה, and טבריה was surrounded by a wall from the days of יהושע בן נון!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 5 using a fact about where רבי lived.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A city that has been walled since the time of יהושע בן נון keeps פורים on the 15th. טבריה is such a city, so רבי was a 'fifteenth' person, not a 'fourteenth' person. That knocks out the previous answer.

keyTerms.meaning: From the days of Joshua son of Nun

phrases.english: Is that so?
But Rebbi was in Tiberias,
and Tiberias was surrounded by a wall
from the days of Joshua son of Nun!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי was a 'fourteenth' person.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: טבריה was walled since the time of יהושע, so its residents keep the 15th.

steps.title: Reverse it: רבי kept the 15th and planted on the 14th
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא flips the answer: רבי kept the 15th and planted on the 14th.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: רבי was a 'fifteenth' person, and when he planted, it was on the fourteenth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps the same idea as before, that רבי planted on a day that was not his פורים, but switches the dates to fit טבריה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: As a resident of walled טבריה, רבי's פורים was the 15th. So the 14th was not his פורים, and planting on it did not break רב יוסף's ban on work. The challenge from step 4 is answered again, this time with the correct dates.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who keeps פורים on the 15th

steps.whatToRemember: רבי planted on the day that was not פורים for him. He lived in walled טבריה, so he kept the 15th and planted on the 14th. That way the planting does not conflict with רב יוסף's teaching that work is forbidden on פורים.

phrases.english: Rather, Rebbi was a "fifteenth" person,
and when he planted — it was on the fourteenth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer of step 5 by reversing the dates, in response to step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reversing the case details to fit the known facts.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי kept the 14th and planted on the 15th.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי kept the 15th, as a resident of טבריה, and planted on the 14th.

steps.title: Was רבי really sure טבריה was walled?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim that רבי was certain טבריה was walled since יהושע בן נון. חזקיה read the מגילה in טבריה on both the 14th and the 15th because he was unsure.
steps.simpleTranslation: Was it really obvious to רבי that טבריה was walled from the days of יהושע בן נון? But חזקיה read the מגילה in טבריה on both the 14th and the 15th, because he was unsure whether it was walled from the days of יהושע בן נון or not!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the reason given in Step 6, that רבי lived in טבריה, which was surely walled. It points out that another great Sage, חזקיה, was not sure about this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7's answer depends on רבי knowing for sure that טבריה is a walled city that keeps the 15th. But חזקיה read on both days, which shows the walled status of טבריה was in doubt. If it was in doubt, how could רבי treat the 14th as an ordinary workday?

keyTerms.meaning: It was obvious / certain to him
He was in doubt about it

phrases.english: And was it obvious to him (Rebbi)
that Tiberias was surrounded by a wall
since the days of Yehoshua bin Nun?
But Chizkiyah would read (the Megillah) in Tiberias
on the fourteenth and on the fifteenth?
He was in doubt
phrases.notes: This explains why חזקיה read on both days.

phrases.aramaic: אִי מוּקֶּפֶת חוֹמָה מִימוֹת יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן הִיא אִי לָא.
phrases.english: whether it was walled since the days of Yehoshua bin Nun or not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the factual premise behind Step 7's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that רבי was certain טבריה was walled since יהושע's time.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: חזקיה's practice of reading on both days shows that the status of טבריה was uncertain.

steps.title: חזקיה was unsure, but רבי was sure
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the doubt was only חזקיה's. רבי himself was certain that טבריה was walled.
steps.simpleTranslation: For חזקיה it was in doubt. For רבי it was obvious.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge simply: different Sages held different views. חזקיה had a doubt, but רבי did not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חזקיה's practice does not prove what רבי knew. Each Sage followed his own understanding, and רבי was certain that טבריה keeps the 15th. So Step 7's answer still works.

phrases.english: To Chizkiyah it was in doubt,
to Rebbi it was obvious.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְחִזְקִיָּה מְסַפְּקָא לֵיהּ, לְרַבִּי פְּשִׁיטָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 8 by separating חזקיה's view from רבי's.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two different Sages held two different views
steps.terutzHavaAmina: חזקיה's doubt suggests that everyone, including רבי, was unsure about טבריה.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי was certain that טבריה was walled, so for him the 14th was not פורים.

steps.title: Even if רבי kept the 15th, isn't the 14th also forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: Even granting that רבי kept only the 15th, the גמרא asks whether he was allowed to work on the 14th. מגילת תענית forbids eulogies on both days, and רבא explained that this means each group may not eulogize on the other group's day.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even if it was obvious to him, was it permitted? It is written in מגילת תענית: the 14th day and the 15th day are days of פורים, and one may not eulogize on them. And רבא said: this was only needed to forbid the people of this day on that day, and the people of that day on this day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new problem. Even if רבי's פורים was the 15th, maybe he still could not work on the 14th.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא teaches that the mention of both days in מגילת תענית makes both days forbidden for everyone, even the day that is not 'yours.' If that is true for eulogies, it should also be true for work. That would make רבי's planting on the 14th forbidden after all.

keyTerms.meaning: An early list of days on which fasting and eulogizing are forbidden
It was needed only for... (explains why a text is not redundant)
Those of this day, on that day

steps.confusionAlert: This is a new and different challenge. Step 8 asked whether רבי was sure which day was his. This step accepts that he was sure, and asks whether keeping the 15th really makes the 14th a permitted workday.

phrases.english: And even if it was obvious to him, is it permitted?
But it is written in Megillat Ta'anit:

phrases.aramaic: אֵת יוֹם אַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר וְאֵת יוֹם חֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר
phrases.english: The fourteenth day and the fifteenth day
are days of Purim,
on which one may not eulogize,
and Rava said: it is needed only

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לֶאֱסוֹר אֶת שֶׁל זֶה בָּזֶה
phrases.english: to forbid the people of this day on that day
and the people of that day on this day?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the answer of Step 9 but brings a new halachic challenge to Step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the 14th is a permitted workday for someone who keeps the 15th.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא reads מגילת תענית as forbidding both days for everyone. Presumably the ban on work also covers both days.

steps.title: The two-day ban covers eulogies and fasting, not work
steps.stepSummary: רבא's rule applies only to eulogizing and fasting. The ban on work applies only to a person's own פורים day.
steps.simpleTranslation: That applies only to eulogies and fasting. But work is forbidden on one day and no more.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by limiting רבא's rule to eulogies and fasting. Work is forbidden only on the day you actually keep פורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא splits the laws of פורים into two kinds. Sad acts like הספד and תענית are forbidden on both days, for everyone. מלאכה is forbidden only on your own day, so רבי could plant on the 14th.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a practical distinction: on the other city's פורים day you may work, but you should not eulogize or fast.

phrases.english: These words apply to eulogy and fasting,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מְלָאכָה — יוֹם אֶחָד וְתוּ לָא.
phrases.english: but labor is forbidden one day and no more.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 10 by narrowing what רבא's rule covers.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of a rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every פורים restriction, including work, applies on both days to everyone.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only eulogies and fasting are forbidden on both days. Work is forbidden only on one's own day.

steps.title: רב cursed a man for planting flax on פורים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea that work is permitted, using a story: רב saw a man planting flax on פורים and cursed him, and the flax never grew.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רב saw a certain man planting flax on פורים, and he cursed him, and his flax did not grow!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story to challenge the claim that work on פורים is not so serious. רב was harsh with someone who planted on פורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's curse shows that planting on פורים was treated as a real wrong. This seems to contradict the lenient picture of Step 11, which said work is allowed on the other day.

phrases.aramaic: אִינִי? וְהָא רַב חַזְיֵיהּ לְהָהוּא גַּבְרָא
phrases.english: Is that so? But Rav saw a certain man
who was planting flax on Purim,
and he cursed him, and his flax did not grow!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי? וְהָא רַב חַזְיֵיהּ לְהָהוּא גַּבְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the leniency about work stated in Step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that work is permitted on the פורים day that is not your own.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A story shows רב treating planting on פורים as a serious wrong.

steps.title: It was that man's own פורים day
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the man in the story planted on his own פורים day, so the work was truly forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it was his day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the story does not contradict the rule. The man planted on the very day he was supposed to keep פורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 said work is forbidden on one day: your own day. The man in רב's story was working on his own פורים, so רב rightly cursed him. רבי planted on the day that was not his, so he did nothing wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: One whose day it was (his own day of פורים)

steps.whatToRemember: On פורים, eulogies and fasting are forbidden on both the 14th and the 15th for everyone. Work is forbidden only on the day you yourself keep פורים. That is why רבי, who kept the 15th in טבריה, could plant on the 14th.

phrases.english: There, it was his (own Purim) day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 12 by showing the story fits the rule of Step 11.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's curse shows that work on any פורים day is forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: The man worked on his own פורים day, which fits the rule that work is forbidden only on one's own day.

steps.title: Even on one's own פורים day, work was never forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רבה בריה דרבא gives a new answer: on פורים the people accepted only the bans on eulogies and fasting, not a ban on work, even on their own day.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה, the son of רבא, said: Even if you say רבי planted on his own פורים day, it was fine. The people accepted upon themselves not to eulogize and not to fast, but they never accepted a ban on work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new way to explain how רבי could plant on פורים. This answer works even if it was רבי's own פורים day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier (Step 11) the answer was that work is banned only on your own פורים day, so רבי must have planted on the other day. רבה בריה דרבא goes further: there is no work ban on פורים at all. Only הספד and תענית were accepted.

keyTerms.meaning: Even if you say (introduces a bolder answer)
On his own day (his own פורים day)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the same answer as Step 11. Step 11 said work is banned only on your own day. Here, work is not banned even on your own day.
steps.whyThisMatters: This becomes the basic view that, by the letter of the law, work on פורים is not forbidden the way it is on a יום טוב.

phrases.english: Rabba, son of Rava, said:
Even if you say it was on his own day —
phrases.notes: Even if רבי planted on his own פורים day.

phrases.english: eulogy and fasting they accepted upon themselves,
labor they did not accept upon themselves.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא בְּיוֹמֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the original question of Step 4. It makes the whole 'planted on the other day' approach (Steps 7–13) unnecessary, because work on פורים was never accepted as forbidden, even on one's own day.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the scope of what was accepted on פורים
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Work is forbidden on one's own פורים day, so רבי must have planted on the other day.
steps.terutzMaskana: Work was never accepted as forbidden on פורים, even on one's own day.

steps.title: Proof from the verses: 'a good day' was dropped
steps.stepSummary: The first proposal for פורים included יום טוב, but the final accepted wording leaves it out. This shows the people never accepted a ban on work.
steps.simpleTranslation: At first the פסוק says: 'gladness and feasting and a good day.' But at the end it says: 'to make them days of feasting and gladness.' The words 'good day' are not written there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves רבה בריה דרבא's claim from the פסוקים in מגילת אסתר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words יום טוב point to a day when work is forbidden. They appear in the first description of פורים but drop out of the final version the people accepted. So the people accepted feasting and joy, but not a ban on work.

keyTerms.meaning: A festival day, when work is forbidden

phrases.english: For at first it is written:
"gladness and feasting and a good day,"
and at the end it is written:
"to make them days of feasting and gladness,"
whereas "a good day" is not written.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports Step 14 with a source.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that a ban on work on פורים was never accepted.
steps.raayaSupportSource: אסתר ט:יט compared with אסתר ט:כב: יום טוב appears in the first verse and is missing from the final one.

steps.title: Then why did רב curse the flax planter?
steps.stepSummary: If work on פורים is allowed, why did רב curse the man who planted flax?
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, why did רב curse that man?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבה בריה דרבא with the story of רב and the flax planter from Step 12.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 13 answered the story by saying the man planted on his own day. Now רבה בריה דרבא says work is fine even on one's own day, so that answer no longer works. The curse needs a new explanation.

phrases.english: But then, what is the reason that Rav
cursed that man?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֶלָּא רַב מַאי טַעְמָא לַטְיֵיהּ לְהָהוּא גַּבְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 14 by bringing back the story of Step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בריה דרבא's view that work on פורים is permitted.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If work is permitted, רב's curse on the flax planter makes no sense.

steps.title: Local custom: the flax planter's town treated it as forbidden
steps.stepSummary: Work is permitted, but in that man's town people had a custom not to work, so he was wrong to break it. In רבי's town there was no such custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was a case of things that are permitted, but other people had a custom to treat them as forbidden. In רבי's place, there was no such custom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב cursed the man for breaking a local custom, not a real law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a rule called דברים המותרין ואחרים נהגו בהן איסור. When people treat a permitted act as forbidden, you may not act otherwise in front of them. The flax planter's town had this custom, but רבי's town did not, so רבי could plant.

keyTerms.meaning: Things that are permitted by law
And others had a custom to treat them as forbidden
In his place, in his town

phrases.english: Things that are permitted,
but others were accustomed to treat them as forbidden — that is what it was.
And in Rabbi's place, they did not have that custom.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבָרִים הַמּוּתָּרִין וַאֲחֵרִים נָהֲגוּ בָּהֶן אִיסּוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 16.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's curse shows that work on פורים is forbidden by law.
steps.terutzMaskana: The curse was for breaking a local custom. רבי's town had no such custom.

steps.title: Second answer: רבי's planting was a planting of joy
steps.stepSummary: Even if רבי's town had the custom not to work, רבי's planting was a 'planting of joy,' which fits the happy spirit of פורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you prefer, say: Really, the custom did exist there. But רבי planted a 'planting of joy.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another way to explain why רבי could plant. Here we assume his town did have the custom not to work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer accepts that the custom existed in רבי's place. רבי's planting was still different: it was planting for enjoyment, not for business. That kind of planting matches the joy of פורים, so it did not break the custom.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces another answer)
A planting of joy, planted for enjoyment rather than profit

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
Actually, they did have the custom —
and Rabbi planted a planting of joy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer, in place of Step 17's claim that רבי's town had no custom.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines the type of act so it falls outside the custom
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the custom existed in רבי's town, his planting would break it.
steps.terutzMaskana: A planting of joy fits the spirit of פורים and is not the work the custom avoids.

steps.title: Proof that 'planting of joy' is a real category
steps.stepSummary: A משנה about fasts for rain lists planting among joyful activities to reduce in hard times. This shows that some planting counts as an act of joy.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: If these fasts passed and the people were not answered, they cut back on business, building, planting, betrothals, and weddings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה to show that planting can be an act of joy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: During a drought, when the community must hold back on happiness, the משנה tells them to reduce planting. It lists planting next to weddings and building. So there is planting that counts as joyful, and that kind of planting fits פורים.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה
These fasts passed and they were not answered

steps.whatToRemember: Work on פורים is not forbidden by law, because יום טוב was left out of the accepted wording. רב's curse is explained by a local custom not to work. רבי's planting was allowed for one of two reasons: either his town had no such custom, or it did have the custom but his planting was a 'planting of joy.'

phrases.english: As we learned in a mishna:
If these fasts passed and they were not answered —
they decrease business,
construction and planting,
betrothals and marriages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the 'planting of joy' idea from Step 18.
steps.raayaObject: That a 'planting of joy' is a real, recognized category.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה in תענית: in times of trouble, planting is reduced along with other joyful activities.

steps.title: A ברייתא defines building and planting of joy
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא on the fast-day משנה explains that the building and planting we cut back on are only the joyful kinds: a wedding house for one's son, and a royal-style pleasure garden.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a ברייתא taught about this משנה: 'building' means building of joy, and 'planting' means planting of joy. What is building of joy? Someone who builds a wedding house for his son. What is planting of joy? Someone who plants a royal pleasure garden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof from the last step. It quotes a ברייתא that defines exactly what 'joyful planting' is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only said 'building' and 'planting.' The ברייתא narrows these to the joyful kinds, not ordinary farming or needed housing. Now we can see what kind of planting רבי did on פורים: planting for pleasure, which matches the joy of the day.

keyTerms.meaning: And a ברייתא taught about it (explaining the משנה)
Planting of joy (planting for pleasure, not food)
A wedding house built for a son's marriage
A royal pleasure garden (shade trees and beauty)

steps.whatToRemember: Work on פורים is allowed in principle. רבי's planting was a joyful planting, like a royal garden, so it fit the spirit of פורים even in a place where people do not work.

phrases.english: And a baraita taught about it:
'Building' means building of joy,
'Planting' means planting of joy.
What is building of joy?
This is one who builds a wedding house for his son.
What is planting of joy?
This is one who plants a royal pleasure garden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof from Step 19 by defining 'planting of joy.'
steps.raayaObject: That רבי's planting on פורים was a 'planting of joy' (Step 18).
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא on the fast-day משנה that defines joyful planting as planting a royal pleasure garden.

steps.title: חזקיה read the מגילה in טבריא on both days
steps.stepSummary: Going back to an earlier statement, the גמרא reports that חזקיה read the מגילה in טבריא on both the 14th and the 15th. He was unsure whether טבריא was walled from the days of יהושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: Back to the statement itself: חזקיה read the מגילה in טבריא on the 14th and the 15th. He was in doubt whether it was surrounded by a wall from the days of יהושע בן נון or not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It goes back to quote and examine an earlier statement about חזקיה in טבריא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unwalled towns read on the 14th, and cities walled since יהושע's time read on the 15th. Since חזקיה was unsure which group טבריא belongs to, he read on both days to be safe. The next steps ask why he was unsure at all.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The matter itself': going back to look at a statement quoted earlier
He was in doubt about it

keyTerms.term: מוּקֶּפֶת חוֹמָה מִימוֹת יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן
keyTerms.meaning: Surrounded by a wall since יהושע's time: such a city reads on the 15th

steps.confusionAlert: חזקיה here is the אמורא, not חזקיהו the king of יהודה.

phrases.english: The matter itself:
Chizkiya read the Megillah in Tiberias
on the fourteenth and on the fifteenth,
because he was in doubt
whether it was surrounded by a wall

phrases.aramaic: מִימוֹת יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן הִיא אִי לָא.
phrases.english: from the days of Joshua son of Nun or not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the פורים-work discussion and examines an earlier statement about חזקיה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חזקיה read the מגילה in טבריא on both the 14th and 15th because he was unsure of its walled status.

steps.title: A verse shows טבריא was a fortified city
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how חזקיה could be unsure. A פסוק in יהושע lists רקת among the fortified cities, and רקת is טבריא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Was he really unsure about טבריא? It is written: 'And the fortified cities were צדים, צר, חמת, רקת and כנרת.' And we hold that רקת is טבריא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges חזקיה's doubt. A פסוק seems to say clearly that טבריא was a walled city in יהושע's time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The book of יהושע calls רקת a 'fortified city,' and we know רקת is טבריא. So טבריא should clearly count as walled since יהושע. Then why would חזקיה be in doubt?

keyTerms.meaning: But was he really in doubt? (opens a challenge)
A city named in יהושע, identified as טבריא

phrases.english: But was he really unsure about the matter of Tiberias?
Isn't it written:
'And the fortified cities were Tziddim, Tzer,
and Chammat, Rakkat, and Kinneret' (Joshua 19:35),
and we hold that Rakkat is Tiberias!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges חזקיה's doubt from Step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: חזקיה's doubt about whether טבריא was walled since יהושע.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק calls רקת (= טבריא) a fortified city in יהושע's time, so there should be no doubt.

steps.title: On one side, the sea was טבריא's wall
steps.stepSummary: The doubt came from the fact that on one side טבריא had no built wall. The sea served as its wall there.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is why he was unsure: on one side, its 'wall' was the sea.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. טבריא was fortified, but not fully by a real wall, because the sea guarded one side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is no longer whether טבריא was fortified. The question is whether a city protected on one side by the sea instead of a built wall counts as 'walled.' That is what made חזקיה unsure.

phrases.english: This is the reason he was in doubt:
because on one side
its wall was the sea.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the doubt: the question is not whether there was a fortification, but whether a sea border counts as a wall.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The doubt was about whether טבריא was fortified at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: טבריא was fortified, but one side was the sea, so it is unclear whether it counts as walled.

steps.title: A ברייתא says the sea is not a wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why there would be any doubt. A ברייתא about houses in walled cities says the word 'סביב' excludes טבריא, because the sea is its wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why was he unsure? The sea is surely not a wall! As a ברייתא taught: 'which has a wall' means a real wall, not a wall of roofs. 'All around' excludes טבריא, whose wall is the sea.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer. A ברייתא already rules that a sea-border city like טבריא does not count as walled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא learns from the פסוקים about selling houses in walled cities that a wall must be a real wall that goes all around. It names טבריא directly as excluded. So the answer of Step 23 seems to leave no room for doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: A 'wall of roofs': houses joined in a ring with no real wall
All around: the wall must fully surround the city

phrases.english: If so, why was he in doubt?
It is certainly not a wall!
As it was taught in a baraita:
'Which has a wall' (Leviticus 25:30), and not a wall of roofs.
'All around' (Leviticus 25:31) excludes Tiberias,
whose sea is its wall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a sea border makes the walled status of טבריא doubtful.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא explicitly excludes טבריא from being a walled city because its wall is the sea, so there is no doubt.

steps.title: The doubt is only about the מגילה: exposed or protected?
steps.stepSummary: For houses in walled cities, טבריא is clearly not walled. For the מגילה, חזקיה did not know which idea defines walled versus unwalled. If it is about being exposed, טבריא is exposed. If it is about being protected, טבריא is protected.
steps.simpleTranslation: For the laws of houses in walled cities he had no doubt. He was unsure about reading the מגילה. What do 'unwalled towns' and 'walled cities' mean in the מגילה? Is it because these are exposed and those are not, and טבריא is also exposed? Or is it because these are protected and those are not, and טבריא is also protected? That is why he was in doubt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא only settles the laws of selling houses. The rule for reading the מגילה may be based on a different idea, so חזקיה's doubt still stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The laws of houses use the word 'סביב,' which requires a full wall all around. The מגילה just says 'פרזים' (unwalled towns), and the reason behind it is unclear. If the point is being open and exposed, טבריא is like an unwalled town and reads on the 14th. If the point is being guarded, the sea protects it, so it is like a walled city and reads on the 15th.

keyTerms.meaning: Houses in walled cities: a Torah law about selling homes

steps.whatToRemember: The same word, 'walled,' can be defined differently in different areas of הלכה. For houses, טבריא is clearly not walled. For the מגילה, it depends on whether the key idea is 'exposed' or 'protected.' That is why חזקיה read on both days.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא is saying טבריא became walled. It is still clearly not walled for houses. The doubt is only about how the מגילה defines a walled city.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a key method: the גמרא does not assume a legal category works the same way everywhere. It asks for the reason behind each law.

phrases.english: Regarding houses of walled cities,
he was not in doubt.
Where he was in doubt
was regarding reading the Megillah:
what are 'unwalled towns' and what are 'walled cities'
that are written regarding reading the Megillah?
Is it because these (unwalled towns) are exposed
and those (walled cities) are not exposed?
If so, this one (Tiberias) is also exposed.
Or perhaps:
it is because these (walled cities) are protected
and those (unwalled towns) are not protected?
If so, this one (Tiberias) is also protected.
Because of this he was in doubt.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעִנְיַן בָּתֵּי עָרֵי חוֹמָה לָא מְסַפְּקָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 24 by limiting the ברייתא to the laws of houses.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Separates two areas of law: the definition of 'walled' for houses does not automatically apply to the מגילה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's ruling that טבריא is not walled applies everywhere, so there is no doubt for the מגילה.
steps.terutzMaskana: For houses, טבריא is clearly not walled. For the מגילה, it depends on whether the rule is about being exposed (then the 14th) or being protected (then the 15th), so חזקיה read on both days.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: חזקיה's doubt was only about the מגילה, because it is unclear whether 'walled' there means 'not exposed' or 'protected.'

steps.title: רב אסי reads the מגילה in הוצל on both days
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי read the מגילה in הוצל on the 14th and the 15th because he was unsure whether הוצל was walled from the days of יהושע בן נון.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אסי read the מגילה in הוצל on the fourteenth and the fifteenth. He was unsure whether it was walled from the days of יהושע בן נון or not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports another case like חזקיה in טבריא. רב אסי read the מגילה on both days in the town of הוצל because he was in doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Walled cities read on the 15th, and unwalled cities read on the 14th. When a city's status is unclear, reading on both days covers both possibilities. חזקיה's doubt came from not knowing how to define a wall. רב אסי's doubt seems to be a question of history: was there a wall back in the days of יהושע or not?

keyTerms.meaning: הוצל, an ancient town in בבל
He was in doubt about it

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a second, different reason a city can end up with a doubtful status. Sometimes the definition is unclear, as with טבריא. Sometimes the history is simply unknown, as with הוצל.

phrases.english: Rav Asi read the Megillah in Huzal
on the fourteenth and on the fifteenth.
He was uncertain about it

phrases.aramaic: אִי מוּקֶּפֶת חוֹמָה מִימוֹת יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן הִיא,
phrases.english: whether it was surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua son of Nun,
or not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel case to חזקיה in טבריא (Step 21). Another אמורא read on both days because of doubt.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a city whose walled status from the days of יהושע is in doubt, one reads the מגילה on both the 14th and the 15th.

steps.title: Another version: רב אסי held הוצל was definitely walled
steps.stepSummary: An alternate report says רב אסי declared that הוצל of בית בנימין was walled from the days of יהושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say a different version: רב אסי said, 'This הוצל of בית בנימין was walled from the days of יהושע.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of רב אסי's view. In this version he was not in doubt at all; he said plainly that הוצל was walled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, רב אסי was unsure and read on both days. In this version, he was certain that הוצל was a walled city, so it would read only on the 15th. The added name 'הוצל of בית בנימין' tells us which הוצל he means.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say (an alternate version of the report)
House of בנימין; used to identify which הוצל is meant

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new opinion arguing with רב אסי. It is a different report of what רב אסי himself held. In one version he was unsure; in the other he was sure.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two versions of רב אסי's view. In the first, הוצל is a doubtful case, so one reads on both days. In the second, הוצל was definitely walled from the days of יהושע.

phrases.english: There are those who say,
Rav Asi said:
This Huzal of the house of Benjamin
was surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents an alternate version of the same report from Step 26, removing the doubt.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to this version, הוצל of בית בנימין is a walled city from the days of יהושע.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן begins a story from his childhood
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן starts to report something he said as a child and later asked the elders about.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: When I was a child, I said something that I later asked the elders about.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. רבי יוחנן introduces a personal story, and the actual content of what he said comes in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is only the opening line. It tells us that רבי יוחנן reached an idea on his own when he was young and then checked it with the older sages. The point of the story comes on the next amud, which connects back to the discussion about טבריא.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
When I was a child
I said something
that I asked the elders about

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: כִּי הֲוֵינָא טַלְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new statement that ties back to the earlier discussion of טבריא. It is a setup line whose content follows on the next amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: This is a setup line only. רבי יוחנן's actual statement follows on the next amud.
